correctness.rationale: The exact factorial-valuation increment decomposes into nonnegative triangular layers for every p≥5. Zero valuation is equivalent to an endpoint condition at every p-power. For indices n<p^r, layers higher than r are automatically zero. The complete digit-lift enumeration gives the claimed recurrences, including a separately proved two-endpoint correction in the p≡5 class; solving with verified initial conditions proves the all-r formula. Every admissible residue has a genuine integer representative, yielding exact covering numbers and box dimension. Independent recurrence computation checked 160861 individual indices across 13 prime cases; finite checks are corroboration, not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The full Frey-Sellers and Cartwright-Kupka accounts already imply a digit-level membership predicate and periodic valuation formula, but do not express the number of surviving indices below p^r. The new all-prime transfer count, with a stable additive boundary correction for p≡5 mod 6 and an explicit p-adic box-counting dimension, is a natural quantitative invariant not stated in the inspected works. Searches failed to locate an equivalent formula; this supports but does not prove historical novelty.
residual_risks: Pointwise divisibility is already completely characterized in 2002 literature; the quantitative closed-form counting theorem is derived from that structural input, so historical importance and priority are narrower than a new primality criterion.

value.rationale: The population of prime-coprime ASM index values is a natural previously unquantified arithmetic statistic of a well-known highly composite sequence. The all-prime exact law distinguishes a two-boundary correction in one congruence class and pure geometric branching in the other; it yields exact sparsity exponent, natural-density zero, and the closure box dimension. These precise mathematical invariants go beyond finite examples or mere algorithmic recomputation and explain the geometry of the prime-coprime index tree.
